---

## Stress-Test: React SPA → React Server Components for Large E-Commerce

---

### Finding 1 — TTFB regression under load annihilates the bundle-size win

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** RSC cuts client-side JavaScript by 40–70%, which should improve FCP and LCP for users on slow devices. Measured benchmarks show LCP improving from 4.1 s to 1.28 s.
- **weakness:** The proposal's implicit premise is that the SPA's bottleneck is *download and parse* of JS. A production SPA served from a global CDN has TTFB of ~20–50 ms (a static file fetch). RSC shifts rendering onto origin servers that must execute React, run data queries, serialize the RSC payload, and stream HTML—*per request*. A reported real-world RSC migration showed TTFB moving from **180 ms median to 620 ms**, with **p95 crossing 1.4 s during moderate traffic**, even as the JS bundle dropped from 420 KB to 110 KB. During peak e-commerce events (Black Friday, flash sales), request volume spikes 5–20×. Without aggressive edge caching, every uncached page hit is a full server render, so TTFB degrades superlinearly. The bundle-size win is meaningless if the first byte arrives 500+ ms later than before.
- **evidence:** Search result summary for the Medium article by Krishnajlathi ("React Server Components Reduced JS. But Our TTFB Went the Wrong Way") reported the 180 ms → 620 ms median TTFB and p95 crossing 1.4 s. The [Web Performance Calendar 2025 article](https://calendar.perfplanet.com/2025/intro-to-performance-of-react-server-components/) separately confirmed LCP improved from 4.1 s to 1.28 s but introduced a **2.52 s interactivity gap** (content visible but non-interactive). The mechanism is sound: a CDN-served static SPA costs ~0 server CPU per request; RSC costs O(page-complexity) CPU per request.
- **falsification:** Run a load test at 2× peak production RPS against the RSC-rendered product listing page. If p95 TTFB stays under 200 ms without edge cache hits, this finding is wrong.
- **severity:** critical
- **confidence:** HIGH

---

### Finding 2 — The interactivity gap creates a "dead-click" window that harms e-commerce conversion

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** Users see content sooner (LCP gains), which is the primary predictor of perceived speed and should improve conversion.
- **weakness:** The proposal assumes visual rendering is the sole conversion driver, but e-commerce pages are *interaction-first*: add-to-cart buttons, size selectors, quantity pickers, search filters, and "Buy Now" actions. The measured interactivity gap after RSC migration was **2.52 seconds** during which the page is visible but non-functional—a classic "uncanny valley of SSR" where users click buttons that do nothing. A pure SPA has **0 s interactivity gap** because nothing renders until JS is ready. Google's research has consistently shown that each 100 ms of interaction delay reduces conversion by ~0.7%. A 2.5 s dead-click window on a product page risks measurable revenue loss. Selective hydration (React 18+ `<Suspense>`) can narrow this gap, but only if the team correctly identifies and wraps every interactive island—an error-prone process at scale.
- **evidence:** The [Web Performance Calendar 2025 article](https://calendar.perfplanet.com/2025/intro-to-performance-of-react-server-components/) measured "the page is not interactive for more than 2 seconds" with RSC, versus 0 s for the client-rendered SPA. The mechanism is structural: RSC streams visible HTML before hydration JS loads and executes.
- **falsification:** Instrument Real User Monitoring (RUM) for First Input Delay (FID) and Interaction to Next Paint (INP) on the RSC-migrated product page. If INP stays under 200 ms within 500 ms of FCP, this finding is invalidated.
- **severity:** critical
- **confidence:** HIGH

---

### Finding 3 — CSS-in-JS dependency forces `"use client"` across the component tree, negating bundle savings

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** RSC eliminates JS for server-rendered components, so even if some components must stay client-side, the net bundle is smaller.
- **weakness:** Large e-commerce React SPAs overwhelmingly use CSS-in-JS libraries (Material UI/MUI, Chakra UI, styled-components, Emotion). These libraries require React's `useContext` hook and browser-side style injection, making them fundamentally incompatible with Server Components. Every component that renders even a single styled element must be marked `"use client"`, which pulls that component *and its entire import subtree* into the client bundle. For a site where MUI or Chakra wraps the layout, nav, product cards, and checkout forms, the practical effect is that the majority of the component tree remains client-rendered. Mux's migration (50,000 lines) identified CSS-in-JS as "probably the biggest part of our RSC conversion," requiring a full migration from styled-components to Tailwind CSS—a massive rework with its own velocity and correctness risks. If the e-commerce site does not migrate off CSS-in-JS, the bundle-size reduction is "underwhelming" (per the Web Performance Calendar measurements of mixed RSC + client-rendering).
- **evidence:** [Josh Comeau's analysis](https://www.joshwcomeau.com/react/css-in-rsc/) confirmed "styled-components are designed to run in-browser…every component that renders even a single styled-component needs to become a Client Component." Mux's [blog post](https://www.mux.com/blog/what-are-react-server-components) on their 50k-line migration called CSS-in-JS "probably the biggest part of our RSC conversion." The [ProNextJS article](https://www.pronextjs.dev/why-doesn-t-material-ui-or-chakra-work-in-the-app-router) confirmed MUI and Chakra require `"use client"` wrapping.
- **falsification:** Audit the current component tree. If fewer than 30% of rendered components by weight depend on CSS-in-JS, this finding's severity drops to medium.
- **severity:** high
- **confidence:** HIGH

---

### Finding 4 — Server-side request waterfalls silently reproduce client-side latency on more expensive hardware

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** Moving data fetching to the server eliminates client-server round-trips and leverages the server's low-latency connection to databases/APIs.
- **weakness:** The hidden assumption is that server-side data fetching is automatically parallel. In practice, RSC components compose hierarchically: a Layout fetches user auth, then a ProductGrid child fetches products, then a RecommendationBar grandchild fetches recommendations. Each `await` in a parent blocks rendering of its children. This recreates the same sequential waterfall that plagued the SPA, but now on server hardware you pay for per-millisecond. As documented by multiple sources, "awaiting data in the parent blocks the entire page. Even if only one section needs the data, your layout, header, and sidebar will still wait." Each sequential hop adds 100–500 ms of database/API latency. With 2–3 stacked `await`s (a common e-commerce pattern: auth → inventory → personalization), the server-side waterfall alone adds 300–1500 ms before streaming even begins.
- **evidence:** [Next.js documentation on data fetching patterns](https://nextjs.org/docs/14/app/building-your-application/data-fetching/patterns) explicitly warns about sequential fetching and recommends parallel patterns. [Aurora Scharff's post](https://aurorascharff.no/posts/avoiding-server-component-waterfall-fetching-with-react-19-cache/) details how to avoid server component waterfall fetching, confirming it is a default failure mode. The [Sentry blog](https://blog.sentry.io/fetch-waterfall-in-react/) documents that waterfalls add "full network latency per step."
- **falsification:** Profile the RSC render path for a product detail page with OpenTelemetry traces. If all data fetches complete within a single 50 ms window (true parallelism), this finding is wrong.
- **severity:** high
- **confidence:** HIGH

---

### Finding 5 — Infrastructure cost model inverts: O(1) CDN becomes O(n) server compute

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** Reduced bandwidth and potential API layer elimination offset the compute cost of server rendering.
- **weakness:** The proposal's implicit cost model assumes rendering cost is negligible. A React SPA served from a CDN is an O(1) infrastructure problem—static assets are cached globally, and the marginal cost per user approaches zero regardless of traffic spikes. RSC rendering is O(n): every uncached page request requires server CPU to execute React components, run data queries, serialize the RSC payload, and stream the response. For a *large* e-commerce site (millions of daily users, with personalized recommendations, geographically-varying pricing, and A/B tests that defeat caching), the proportion of cache-miss requests is high. No credible source provides a concrete TCO comparison; the [FullStackTechies article](https://fullstacktechies.com/react-server-components-rsc-for-enterprise/) claims "25–40% reduction in hosting costs" but supplies zero supporting data. Meanwhile, the same article acknowledges RSC "shifts the CPU burden from the user's device to the server." For personalized e-commerce pages, aggressive caching is impossible, and every request is a server render.
- **evidence:** Reasoning chain: SPA + CDN → static asset, served from edge, cost is bandwidth only (~$0.01–0.08/GB on major CDNs). RSC + personalization → per-request server render, cost is compute (~$0.00004/vCPU-second on AWS Lambda). At 100M page views/month with 200 ms average render time, that's ~55,000 vCPU-hours/month ($2,200+ on Lambda, more on provisioned infrastructure). The SPA CDN cost for the same traffic would be dominated by API calls that *both* architectures must make. The marginal rendering cost exists only in RSC. The [FullStackTechies source](https://fullstacktechies.com/react-server-components-rsc-for-enterprise/) cost claims are [unverified]—no methodology or data backs them.
- **falsification:** Deploy the RSC version behind a cost-monitoring proxy for one week at production traffic. If total compute + bandwidth cost is ≤ 120% of current SPA + API cost, this finding is wrong.
- **severity:** high
- **confidence:** MEDIUM (cost numbers are estimated, not measured)

---

### Finding 6 — Known DoS vulnerabilities in RSC deserialization create an attack surface that the SPA never had

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** All software has vulnerabilities; these are patched, and mature teams apply security updates promptly.
- **weakness:** The proposal introduces a *net-new* attack surface: the RSC Server Functions endpoint accepts and deserializes user-controlled HTTP payloads. Three CVEs (CVE-2025-55184, CVE-2025-67779, CVE-2026-23864, all CVSS 7.5 High) allow a specially crafted request to trigger infinite loops, server crashes, or out-of-memory exceptions—even if no custom Server Functions are defined. A fourth CVE (CVE-2025-55183, CVSS 5.3) enables source code and hardcoded secret leakage. A pure SPA has no server-side React execution surface; the only attack vector is the API layer, which is already hardened. The RSC architecture adds a second server-side deserialization endpoint that must be independently secured, monitored, and patched in perpetuity. For a large e-commerce site, a DoS on the rendering tier takes down the entire storefront—not just an API endpoint.
- **evidence:** [React.dev security advisory (2025-12-11)](https://react.dev/blog/2025/12/11/denial-of-service-and-source-code-exposure-in-react-server-components) confirmed the vulnerabilities affect `react-server-dom-webpack`, `react-server-dom-parcel`, and `react-server-dom-turbopack` versions 19.0.0–19.2.3. The [Socket.dev analysis](https://socket.dev/blog/new-react-server-components-vulnerabilities-dos-and-source-code-exposure) confirmed the scope. Patched in 19.0.4, 19.1.5, 19.2.4, but the *class* of vulnerability (deserialization of untrusted input) is structural and likely to recur.
- **falsification:** If the RSC Server Functions endpoint is behind a WAF that rate-limits and validates request payloads, and no Server Functions are exported, the practical exploitability drops. Demonstrate that the endpoint is unreachable from the public internet without authentication.
- **severity:** high
- **confidence:** HIGH

---

### Finding 7 — State management rearchitecture is a forced, unplanned migration-within-a-migration

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** Modern state management (TanStack Query, Zustand, Jotai) works well with RSC when properly separated into server-state and client-state layers.
- **weakness:** The proposal implicitly assumes the existing SPA's state management is portable. In practice, large React SPAs accumulate deep dependencies on Redux, Zustand, or React Context for cross-cutting concerns: cart state, user authentication, feature flags, A/B test assignments, locale/currency, and notification state. None of these can run in Server Components (no hooks, no context, no state). The migration therefore forces a complete rearchitecture of state management: separating what must stay client-side from what can be server-derived, replacing Context-based theming, and potentially migrating from Redux to a server-state/client-state split architecture. This is not a refactor—it is a parallel architectural migration with its own correctness risks (state synchronization bugs between server-rendered and client-hydrated components) and velocity cost. Mux explicitly reported that "every time a new developer picked up our codebase, the questions came up: 'What's running on the server? What's running on the client?'"
- **evidence:** [Mux blog](https://www.mux.com/blog/what-are-react-server-components): "You can access React Context only in Client Components," which forced workarounds. [Zustand GitHub discussion #2200](https://github.com/pmndrs/zustand/discussions/2200) discusses misuse of Zustand in Server Components. The [React.dev docs on Server Components](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components) confirm hooks and context are unavailable.
- **falsification:** If the current SPA already uses a server-state/client-state split (e.g., TanStack Query for server data, minimal client-only state), and uses zero React Context for cross-cutting concerns, this finding's severity drops to low.
- **severity:** high
- **confidence:** HIGH

---

### Finding 8 — RSC payload + HTML duality creates a cache-consistency hazard that SPAs don't have

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** Next.js handles RSC caching automatically, and Partial Prerendering (PPR) lets the static shell be edge-cached while dynamic parts stream.
- **weakness:** RSC produces *two* artifacts per page: an HTML response (for initial loads) and an RSC payload (for client-side navigations). These must be cache-invalidated atomically; if a CDN serves HTML from render A and an RSC payload from render B, users see stale or mismatched content during navigation. The [Contentstack documentation on handling Next.js RSC issues](https://www.contentstack.com/docs/developers/launch/handling-nextjs-rsc-issues-on-launch) confirms this is a production problem. For an e-commerce site, a cache mismatch can show wrong prices, out-of-stock items appearing available, or stale promotional banners—all correctness bugs with revenue and trust impact. An SPA has a single cache artifact (the static bundle) plus API responses; cache consistency is a solved problem.
- **evidence:** [Next.js caching documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/caching) states that "HTML response and the RSC Payload" are stored together, and warns about platform caches that might separate them. The [Contentstack article](https://www.contentstack.com/docs/developers/launch/handling-nextjs-rsc-issues-on-launch) describes real-world RSC caching issues on launch. Mechanism: any CDN or reverse proxy (Cloudflare, Akamai, Varnish) that caches independently by URL without custom `Vary` header handling will break this invariant.
- **falsification:** If the deployment uses Vercel's native hosting (which manages RSC caching atomically), or a CDN configuration that is verified to invalidate both artifacts together, this finding is mitigated. Test: perform a content update, then immediately do both a fresh page load and a client-side navigation; confirm content is identical.
- **severity:** medium
- **confidence:** HIGH

---

### Finding 9 — Developer velocity degrades measurably during and after the migration

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** The migration is a one-time cost that pays off in long-term velocity through simpler data fetching and smaller bundles.
- **weakness:** The proposal assumes velocity impact is transient. Evidence suggests it is structural. Developers must continuously reason about the server/client boundary for every component, every prop, and every import. Mux reported ongoing PR review friction ("frequent PR feedback about unnecessary client-side code shipping"), debugging difficulty ("requiring console.log verification" of execution environment), and onboarding overhead ("every time a new developer picked up our codebase"). The 2024 React survey showed that "almost all pain points" were related to RSCs and adjacent technologies. For a large e-commerce team (20–50+ engineers, frequent hires), the permanent cognitive overhead of the server/client boundary is a tax on every feature shipped. Additionally, tripled build times were reported during migration—directly slowing iteration speed.
- **evidence:** [Mux blog](https://www.mux.com/blog/what-are-react-server-components) on ongoing cognitive overhead. The [Medium migration article by Deval Kasundra](https://medium.com/@deval93/react-server-components-what-they-dont-tell-you-about-migration-part-1-acdfdd80f157) reported "cryptic errors, tripled build times." Community survey data (cited in search results) showed only 29% of React developers have used RSCs despite 50%+ positive sentiment—suggesting a gap between aspiration and successful adoption.
- **falsification:** Track team-level cycle time (PR open → merge) for 3 months post-migration. If it returns to within 10% of pre-migration baseline and onboarding time for new engineers doesn't increase, this finding is wrong.
- **severity:** medium
- **confidence:** HIGH

---

### Acceptance Condition

The migration is acceptable **if and only if** all of the following hold simultaneously:

1. **TTFB under load** stays ≤ 200 ms at p95 during peak traffic (verified via load test at 2× Black Friday levels), through edge caching or PPR.
2. **Interactivity gap** (INP within 500 ms of FCP) stays under 200 ms, verified via RUM on critical conversion paths (PDP, cart, checkout).
3. **The existing CSS-in-JS library** is either already absent or the team budgets a full migration to a zero-runtime CSS solution (Tailwind, CSS Modules) *before* the RSC migration, not concurrently.
4. **Server-side data fetching** is profiled with distributed tracing and verified to be parallel, not waterfall.
5. **Infrastructure cost** is projected and load-tested with realistic personalization-driven cache-miss rates (expect 40–70% miss for logged-in users).
6. **RSC package versions** are ≥ 19.0.4/19.1.5/19.2.4, and the Server Functions endpoint is behind rate-limiting and input validation.
7. **State management rearchitecture** is scoped and budgeted as a separate workstream with its own QA plan.
8. **CDN caching** is validated to atomically invalidate HTML and RSC payloads.

If any of these conditions cannot be met, the migration should be scoped to static, non-personalized pages only (product category pages, blog, about)—not the interactive core of the e-commerce experience.

Here is the full stress-test of the RSC migration proposal.

---

## Finding 1 — Bundle Size Reduction Premise Collapses for Interaction-Heavy E-Commerce UIs

**target:** the proposal

**steelman:** React Server Components eliminate JavaScript for components that render only on the server, so a large product catalog page with static HTML rendering genuinely ships no component code to the browser — measurably reducing bundle size and parse time.

**weakness:** A large e-commerce site is structurally interaction-heavy. Product image carousels, real-time inventory badges, add-to-cart buttons, variant selectors, cart drawers, Stripe Elements, Algolia instant search, live chat widgets, and A/B testing scaffolding all require browser APIs, event handlers, or third-party SDKs that use `useLayoutEffect` or global browser objects — and every such dependency forces a `"use client"` boundary. When the `"use client"` directive is placed on shared component files high in the component tree (the natural resolution when a build error surfaces), it promotes that entire subtree to a Client Component, silently erasing every bundle saving RSC was supposed to deliver. The architectural complexity of maintaining the server/client split remains while the performance benefit disappears entirely. On a large site with accumulated third-party integrations, this is not an edge case — it is the default outcome without sustained architectural discipline.

**evidence:** "Every component is a Client Component. Every component ships JavaScript to the client. The RSC architecture is in place — the routing, the layout, the page files — but the actual benefit (JavaScript that never ships) is zero. You've added the complexity of the Server/Client boundary, the mental overhead of 'use client' everywhere, and the security surface of Server Actions — for a bundle size identical to before." (LogRocket via WebFetch) | Reasoning chain: e-commerce interaction surface → third-party library incompatibility → `"use client"` propagation → zero bundle reduction + full RSC complexity cost. Confidence: HIGH.

**falsification:** Audit the migrated app's webpack bundle after migration. If the JS shipped to the browser is ≥ 90% of the pre-migration bundle size, the premise has failed. Tool: `next/bundle-analyzer` before and after.

**severity:** critical
**confidence:** HIGH

---

## Finding 2 — Dynamic RSC Navigation Requests Systematically Bypass CDN, Eliminating Horizontal Scalability

**target:** the proposal

**steelman:** RSC payloads are small, serialized JSON-like streams; a CDN should cache them like any other HTTP response, distributing load away from origin and keeping latency low under high traffic.

**weakness:** When a user navigates client-side in a Next.js RSC app, the framework appends a `?_rsc=<hash>` query parameter to the request. Critically, this hash is derived from the *navigation history* (the origin route's state tree), not the destination page's content. The result is that two users navigating to the same `/product/123` page from different origins generate different `_rsc` values, producing unique cache keys that CDNs treat as separate, un-cacheable resources. For a large e-commerce site — which is exactly the high-traffic, product-catalog-heavy case — this means every client-side navigation to a dynamic page hits the origin server directly. The CDN, the primary scalability mechanism for an SPA that can serve a static JS bundle to millions of users, is bypassed for the most common user interaction: browsing the catalog. The `Vary: RSC, Next-Router-State-Tree, Next-Router-Prefetch, Next-Url` response header where `Next-Router-State-Tree` reflects the origin page compounds this: even if a CDN attempted to cache by destination, it cannot deduplicate by origin. This also means every deployment-triggered hash change breaks any cached RSC payloads in flight, requiring CDN purge coordination.

**evidence:** "Every time a user moves to a dynamic page, RSC makes different /xxx?_rsc=yyy requests with different _rsc hash, and those _rsc requests have absolutely no cache, meaning CDN ignores them and pass them directly to the server, even if the full page is cached on the CDN." (GitHub vercel/next.js Discussion #59167, fetched directly) | "Responses include headers like 'Vary: RSC, Next-Router-State-Tree, Next-Router-Prefetch, Next-Url' where 'Next-Router-State-Tree' reflects the origin page, not the destination, undermining CDN caching effectiveness." (ibid.) Confidence: HIGH.

**falsification:** Enable CDN logging (Cloudflare Cache Analytics or equivalent) on a staging deployment. Measure cache hit ratio for `?_rsc=*` requests during a simulated browse session traversing 20 product pages from 3 different entry points. A hit ratio above 60% would falsify this finding.

**severity:** critical
**confidence:** HIGH

---

## Finding 3 — Subsequent Navigation Latency Regresses Relative to the Replaced SPA for High-Frequency Browse Patterns

**target:** the proposal

**steelman:** RSC prefetching on link hover or viewport entry pre-warms RSC payloads before the user clicks, making navigations feel instantaneous. The SPA required full JS execution per component on first load too; RSC just shifts the work.

**weakness:** In a pure SPA, after the initial JS bundle is downloaded and cached (browser cache, service worker), all subsequent navigations are entirely client-side state transitions: 80ms in measured benchmarks for in-memory routing. The JS bundle does not change between navigations; no network request is made. In RSC, every navigation to a dynamic route — and all personalized e-commerce pages are dynamic (user-specific cart, regional pricing, live inventory) — requires a network round-trip to origin for the RSC payload, because (a) the payload is user-specific and cannot be shared, (b) the `_rsc` hash prevents CDN caching as established above, and (c) prefetching all links on a category page listing 48 products would require 48 concurrent RSC requests, creating server load that defeats the prefetch strategy. The measured SPA navigation time of 80ms documented in a direct benchmark is not achievable with any server round-trip on commodity connections. Additionally, the article documents that the App Router "seems to delay all JavaScript until after the CSS is loaded," extending the interactivity gap beyond what the Pages Router achieved.

**evidence:** "transitions between pages when everything is on the client and there is no back-and-forth with the server can be incredibly fast. In the case of this project, navigating from the Inbox page to Settings takes just 80ms." (Nadia Makarevich / developerway.com, fetched via Medium mirror) | "any dynamic logic blocks the transition and makes navigation feel heavy" (WebSearch summary of perfplanet.com/2025 article, attributed to the blocking-layouts failure mode). Reasoning: server round-trip latency on p95 connections (100-200ms RTT) structurally exceeds 80ms SPA navigation; personalization forces all key pages to be dynamic. Confidence: HIGH.

**falsification:** Measure client-side navigation time (Navigation Timing API, `navigationStart` to `domInteractive`) for 10 product→product transitions in the SPA baseline vs. the RSC migration on the same connection profile (simulated 4G). If RSC p95 navigation time is ≤ 150ms (SPA + one RTT acceptable overhead), this finding is mitigated.

**severity:** high
**confidence:** HIGH

---

## Finding 4 — Client-Side Router Cache Delivers Stale Inventory and Pricing Data by Default

**target:** the proposal

**steelman:** Next.js provides `revalidatePath` and `revalidateTag` APIs for on-demand cache invalidation. A well-implemented mutation pipeline calls these after any data change, ensuring users always see current stock and pricing.

**weakness:** Next.js maintains a *client-side* Router Cache separate from the server-side Data Cache and Full Route Cache. This cache holds RSC payloads in the browser tab for 30 seconds (dynamic routes) or 5 minutes (static routes) and is not automatically invalidated by a server-side `revalidatePath` call — because the server has no channel to push invalidation to an already-loaded client tab. A user who loads a product page, stays on the tab, and the product goes out of stock (or a flash sale starts) will continue to see the stale "In Stock" / original price for up to 30 seconds even though the server cache has been correctly invalidated. For e-commerce, this is a correctness failure with direct revenue implications: overselling out-of-stock items, or users being charged the wrong price. The fix (`router.refresh()`) requires explicit developer action on every mutation path, which is easy to omit. The earlier Next.js GitHub deep-dive discussion acknowledges "clicking on a link not loading a fresh view of the data is unintuitive" even for developers who understand the system.

**evidence:** Router cache durations: "Static routes: 5 minutes of client-side cache. Dynamic routes: 30 seconds of client-side cache." (GitHub vercel/next.js Discussion #54075, fetched directly.) | "the Router Cache in the browser tab might still have the previous result from the server, instead of the very latest data" after `revalidatePath` / `revalidateTag` (WebSearch summary from dev.to/pockit_tools and GitHub #59167). | "The Router Cache can lead to stale data being displayed as pages are not requested from the server again during navigation." (ibid.) Confidence: HIGH for the mechanism; MEDIUM for the 30s/5m values, which were confirmed in the #54075 thread but may not reflect the most current Next.js 16 default.

## Finding 5 — Sequential `await` in Nested Server Components Creates Server-Side Waterfalls That Worsen Response Latency vs. Parallel SPA Fetches

**target:** the proposal

**steelman:** RSC moves data fetching to the server, colocating fetches with components and eliminating client-server round-trip overhead. Because fetches happen server-to-service (low latency), they resolve faster than browser-to-API calls.

**weakness:** The idiomatic RSC pattern of writing `await fetchProduct()` in a parent server component and `await fetchReviews()` in a child that is rendered by the parent creates a strict sequential dependency: the child cannot start fetching until the parent has resolved and rendered. On a product detail page with 4–5 data sources (product details, reviews, related products, inventory status, user personalization), this creates a server-side waterfall with total latency equal to the *sum* of all fetch times, not the maximum. The equivalent SPA pattern fires all API calls in parallel on component mount, with individual loading skeletons, so total latency equals the *maximum* of all fetch times — structurally faster. ### Finding 1 — CDN Bypass on Client-Side Navigation Destroys Horizontal Scalability Under Load

- **target:** Analyst A (Finding 2) — incorporated and extended
- **steelman:** RSC payloads are lightweight serialized streams and should be cacheable at CDN edges, preserving the SPA's O(1) scalability for repeat visitors. The Next.js team is actively moving toward pathname-based cache keying that would resolve this.
- **weakness:** Today, every client-side navigation to a dynamic RSC route appends a `?_rsc=<hash>` parameter derived from the user's *origin router state*, not the destination content. Two users requesting the same `/product/123` from different preceding pages generate different cache keys. The official Next.js CDN caching guide (v16.2.6, last updated 2026-05-28) acknowledges the `Vary: RSC, Next-Router-State-Tree, Next-Router-Prefetch, Next-Url` header set and states pathname-based keying is merely "in active design"—it has not shipped. For a high-traffic e-commerce catalog where users freely browse (48-product category pages → product detail → back → next page), the CDN hit ratio on RSC navigation payloads approaches zero for personalized (logged-in) sessions. Every miss hits origin. Combined with the TTFB cost of server-rendering RSC (my Finding 1 from the prior round), this creates superlinear latency degradation under peak load. The SPA baseline has no equivalent failure mode: its static bundle is immutably CDN-cached and navigations are zero-network-cost state transitions.
- **evidence:** Next.js official documentation (fetched 2026-05-31) states: "For routes without PPR, the `next-router-state-tree` header is read during prefetch requests to determine which segments to include, which increases cache `vary` as it passes the current router state." The same doc confirms pathname-based keying's "current status" is "in active design" — not shipped. [GitHub vercel/next.js Discussion #59167](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/59167) confirms the production impact. [Next.js CDN Caching Guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/cdn-caching).
- **falsification:** Enable Partial Prerendering (PPR) on all catalog routes. If PPR-enabled static prefetch responses achieve >80% CDN hit ratio under realistic browse patterns (verified via CDN analytics), the issue is mitigated for the critical path.
- **severity:** critical
- **confidence:** HIGH

### Finding 2 — TTFB Regression Under Peak Traffic Negates Bundle-Size Savings

- **target:** the proposal
- **steelman:** Removing 40–60% of client JS improves FCP and LCP on slow devices; the reduced parse/execute time dominates the user experience improvement.
- **weakness:** The implicit premise is that download+parse of JS is the primary bottleneck. A production SPA served from a CDN edge has TTFB of ~20–50 ms (static file). RSC shifts rendering to origin: execute React, resolve data queries, serialize RSC payload, and stream. Published migration data reports median TTFB moving from 180 ms to 620 ms, with p95 crossing 1.4 s during moderate traffic. During peak e-commerce events (Black Friday: 5–20× traffic spikes), every cache-miss RSC request hits compute. Combined with Finding 1 (CDN bypass for navigations), this means origin servers absorb both initial page loads AND navigation requests that a CDN would previously have handled. The bundle-size win (saving ~200 ms of parse time) is overwhelmed by 400+ ms additional TTFB.

- **confidence:** HIGH

### Finding 7 — Streaming Mid-Render Errors Cannot Return Proper HTTP Status Codes, Breaking Monitoring and SEO

- **target:** the proposal (new finding)
- **steelman:** Error boundaries in Next.js (`error.tsx`) catch component failures gracefully, and streaming enables progressive rendering that tolerates partial failures without crashing the page.
- **weakness:** HTTP streaming commits to a `200 OK` status code *before* the component tree has fully resolved. If a component throws after the stream has begun (e.g., an inventory service is down, a pricing API times out), Next.js *cannot* change the HTTP status to 500 or 404 — the headers have already been sent. The framework injects a `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` tag and performs client-side error recovery, but: (a) monitoring systems that rely on HTTP status codes (Datadog, PagerDuty synthetic checks, CDN error rate dashboards) will report 200 for what is actually a broken page; (b) search engines that crawl before the meta tag is injected may index broken content; (c) `redirect()` called mid-stream becomes a client-side redirect instead of a proper 301/302, breaking SEO link equity transfer. For e-commerce, where SEO drives 30–60% of organic traffic and monitoring is critical for uptime SLAs, this is a correctness and observability failure mode the SPA doesn't have (SPA API errors are separate from page delivery and have proper status codes).
- **evidence:** Search results confirmed: "When a Suspense fallback renders or a component suspends, the server must commit to 200 OK in order to start sending the HTML stream. If a notFound() fires mid-stream, Next.js cannot go back and change the status to 404." "Similarly, a redirect() mid-stream becomes a client-side redirect rather than an HTTP redirect header." Additionally, [GitHub Discussion #48381](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/48381) documents unresolved stream abort handling — the discussion has no official solution as of 2024.
- **falsification:** Configure synthetic monitoring to parse response bodies (not just status codes) for error indicators. If the team implements body-level health checks AND uses `onShellError` to catch all pre-stream errors (returning proper 500s before headers are committed), the practical impact is reduced. Verify by intentionally killing the inventory service and confirming monitoring alerts fire within SLA.

- **confidence:** HIGH

### Finding 1 — Bundle-Size Premise Structurally Collapses for Interaction-Heavy Commerce UIs

**target:** the proposal

**steelman:** RSC genuinely eliminates JavaScript for components that render exclusively on the server. A product catalog rendered server-side ships zero component JS to the browser — measurably improving parse time on low-end devices.

**weakness:** Every feature of a large e-commerce site that users interact with — add-to-cart buttons, variant selectors, quantity pickers, Stripe Elements, real-time inventory badges, Algolia instant search, live chat overlays, A/B testing scaffolding — requires browser APIs or event handlers and forces a `"use client"` boundary. When third-party library incompatibilities surface during build (the default for mature SPAs using Material UI, Chakra, Emotion, or styled-components), the natural resolution is placing `"use client"` high on a shared component file. This silently promotes the entire import subtree to client components, erasing every bundle saving while the full RSC architectural complexity cost (server/client boundary reasoning, async component constraints, router cache management) remains. The net outcome is a larger engineering surface area for an unchanged bundle.

**evidence:** "Every component is a Client Component. Every component ships JavaScript to the client. The RSC architecture is in place — the routing, the layout, the page files — but the actual benefit (JavaScript that never ships) is zero." **falsification:** Run `@next/bundle-analyzer` on the migrated build. If the client JS bundle is ≥ 90% of the pre-migration baseline, the premise has failed regardless of what the architecture diagram says.

### Finding 5 — Client-Side Router Cache Delivers Stale Inventory and Pricing; Server-Side `revalidatePath` Cannot Push Invalidation to Open Tabs

**target:** the proposal

**steelman:** Next.js provides `revalidatePath`, `revalidateTag`, and on-demand ISR. A properly instrumented mutation pipeline ensures stale data windows are bounded and acceptable for e-commerce SLAs.

**weakness:** The Next.js client-side Router Cache stores RSC payloads in the browser tab for 30 seconds (dynamic routes). This cache is separate from the server Data Cache and is not reachable by `revalidatePath` — because the server has no push channel to an already-loaded tab. A user who loads a product page, keeps the tab open, and an inventory change occurs (flash sale ends, stock depletes) will see stale "In Stock" and original pricing for up to 30 seconds even after the server correctly invalidates its own caches. The fix is `router.refresh()` called explicitly at every mutation point — an engineering discipline that is easy to omit on a large team across hundreds of mutation paths. For e-commerce, this is not a UX nuisance; it is a revenue and correctness failure: overselling out-of-stock items, presenting expired promotional prices.

(Multiple sources, WebSearch-confirmed.) Mechanism: HTTP-level cache invalidation cannot reach in-browser JS memory state; only explicit `router.refresh()` does. Confidence: HIGH.

**falsification:** Mark a product out-of-stock server-side and call `revalidateTag`. Without a hard browser refresh, navigate away and back within 30 seconds. If the page shows updated stock, the router cache is being correctly bypassed — test passes. Failing result is the expected default without explicit `router.refresh()` instrumentation.

### Finding 6 — Server-Side Fetch Waterfall Is the Default RSC Composition Pattern and Adds Additive Latency

**target:** the proposal

**steelman:** Server-to-service latency (10–30ms to a co-located database) is far lower than browser-to-API latency (100–300ms). Even with sequential fetches, the absolute latency is lower than the parallel SPA equivalent.

The server-to-service latency advantage is real but does not overcome the additive-vs.-maximum structural difference at scale.
